abstract: Virtual studios have been demonstrated at broadcast exhibitions since their first showing at IBC in 1994. They created an immediate impact because program producers were excited by both the technology and the potential for enhancing their own productions. Subsequent to the initial euphoria, it was soon realized that not only did these virtual studios require substantial amounts of computing power, but also needed a number of specialist staff to operate and design the virtual sets. Could a lower cost, simpler alternative be found? This paper will discuss the requirements for operating a low cost two-dimensional (2-D) virtual studio. It offers a ground-up approach on how virtual programs can be designed and produced, starting from a conventional studio or chroma-key facility. The vital components for any virtual studio will be introduced and described, as will the potential benefits of using a virtual set.

authors.bio: David Drew is the product manager for the Virtual Scenario Studio System. This hardware solution to virtual productions was developed in conjunction with the BBC Research Dept. and is manufactured by Radamec Broadcast Systems in the U.K. After studying electronic engineering at Brunei University, his career in the broadcast industry began in 1984 with the BBC, where he was trained in the fundamentals of television studio engineering and operations. Practical operations experience was gained while working on the then new breakfast program, as well as other news and current affairs programs. He has also worked for video effects and television camera equipment manufacturers. This experience enabled him to give the Royal Television Society engineering training lectures on “The Television Camera.” Recent publications include “Virtual Scenario” in International Broadcast Engineer, March 1996, and “Designing Sets for Virtual Studios” in TVB Europe, March 1997.
